flawed_step: Step 5: planarity does not force a singleton-colored neighbor to have a Kempe component, with the repeated color, containing neither repeated-color neighbor.
counterexample: Let V(G)={v,u1,u2,u3,u4,u5}. Join v to every ui. Add the cycle u1u2u3u4u5u1 and edges u2u4,u2u5. This is planar: draw the cycle with v and its spokes inside and the two noncrossing edges u2u4,u2u5 outside. Color (u1,u2,u3,u4,u5)=(1,2,1,3,4). The coloring is proper. The bichromatic components meeting the neighbors are: for 1/2, {u1,u2,u3}; for 1/3, {u1} and {u3,u4}; for 1/4, {u1,u5} and {u3}; and for 2/3, 2/4, and 3/4, respectively {u2,u4}, {u2,u5}, and {u4,u5}. Swapping either color pair on any one listed component leaves all four colors represented among u1,...,u5.
assessment_summary:
Complete proof attempt and audit:
1. The five neighbors use all four colors, so one color r occurs twice and three colors p,q,s occur once each. JUSTIFIED: the only positive distribution of five occurrences among four colors is (2,1,1,1).
2. Let x,x' be the r-colored neighbors and let yp,yq,ys be the uniquely p-, q-, and s-colored neighbors. JUSTIFIED: this is notation supplied by Step 1.
3. If, for two singleton colors p and q, yp and yq lie in different components of the p/q-induced subgraph, interchange p and q on the component containing yp. Then p disappears from the neighborhood. JUSTIFIED: yp is the only p-colored neighbor, while the only q-colored neighbor is outside the swapped component, so the swap introduces no p on the neighborhood.
4. Consequently, it remains only to consider the case in which every pair among yp,yq,ys is connected in its corresponding two-color subgraph. JUSTIFIED: otherwise Step 3 proves the desired conclusion.
5. Attempted planar step: in that remaining case, planarity forces some t in {p,q,s} such that the r/t-component containing yt contains neither x nor x'. NOT JUSTIFIED: the asserted separation consequence does not follow from planarity. In the counterexample, the singleton vertices are pairwise Kempe-connected, while the 1/2-component contains both repeated-color neighbors and the 1/3- and 1/4-components containing the singleton neighbor each contain one repeated-color neighbor.
6. If the component claimed in Step 5 existed, swapping it would remove t from the neighborhood. CONDITIONALLY JUSTIFIED, BUT UNAVAILABLE: yt would change from t to r and neither r-colored neighbor would change to t, but Step 5 has not established such a component.
7. One could then color v with t. CONDITIONALLY JUSTIFIED, BUT UNAVAILABLE: a color absent from the neighborhood may properly be assigned to v, but Step 6 was not obtained.
8. For an independent check, construct the six-vertex graph and coloring described in counterexample. JUSTIFIED: the indicated inside/outside drawing proves planarity, v has degree 5, and every listed edge has differently colored endpoints.
9. For colors 1/2, 2/3, 2/4, and 3/4, the relevant neighbors of both colors lie in one component. JUSTIFIED: the respective connecting edges are u1u2,u2u3; u2u4; u2u5; and u4u5.
10. Swapping any of those four components merely permutes two colors that both remain represented. JUSTIFIED: each component contains every neighbor having either of its two colors.
11. For colors 1/3, the components are {u1} and {u3,u4}; for colors 1/4, they are {u1,u5} and {u3}. Swapping any one of them also preserves all four neighborhood colors. JUSTIFIED: direct inspection shows that one color-1 neighbor remains while both interchanged colors remain represented.
12. These six color pairs exhaust every permitted Kempe interchange, so no single interchange leaves at most three colors on the neighborhood. JUSTIFIED: a four-coloring has exactly six unordered pairs of distinct colors, all checked in Steps 9–11. Thus the proposed statement is false.
